Paper_name: Self-relevance and the activation of attentional networks
Summary: This study used arbitrary geometric shapes and the Attention Network Test (ANT) to establish the extent to which self-relevance (vs friend-relevance) moderates the three subsystems of attentional functioning: alerting, orienting, and executive control. Participants first completed a shape-label matching task associating shapes with the self and a best friend, then completed the ANT. Only executive control was sensitive to the meaning of the stimuli: conflict resolution was enhanced following self-associated compared with friend-associated shapes (cues). A Shrinking Spotlight Diffusion Model analysis indicated that self-relevance facilitated the narrowing of visual attention.
Author: Saga Svensson, Marius Golubickis, Sam Johnson, Johanna K. Falbén, C. Neil Macrae
Conclusion: The personal significance of otherwise trivial material modulates attentional processing: self-relevance influences the executive control network (conflict resolution) and facilitates the narrowing of visual attention, rather than globally modulating all attentional networks.
